senses: mouth, lips, opening, entrance, aperture, orifice
la:noun:os.html:
ōs, ōris (no
gen. plur.), n.
kindr. with Sanscr. āsya, os, vultus, facies
, the mouth (syn. bucca): quam tibi ex ore orationem duriter dictis dedit, Enn. ap. : ex ore in ejus os inflato aquam dato palumbo,: ad haec omnia percipienda os est aptissimum,: oris hiatus,: os tenerum pueri,: fetidum,: trilingue,: os loquentis Opprimere,: in ore omnium esse, to be in everybody's mouth, to be the common talk: in ore est omni populo,: istius nequitiam in ore vulgi atque in communibus proverbiis esse versatam,: Harmodius in ore est,: in ore omnium,: habere aliquid in ore,to have a thing in one's mouth, be constantly talking of it,; ; ; : poscebatur ore vulgi dux Agricola,with one voice, one consent, unanimously,.—So, uno ore, unanimously, ; ; ; ; : uno omnes eadem ore fremebant,: volito vivus per ora virūm, soon become famous, Enn. ap. (Epigr. v. 4 Vahl.): virūm volitare per ora,: in ora vulgi, or hominum pervenire, or abire,to get into people's mouths, become the common talk,; : ire per ora Nomen,: hic Graecā doctrinā ore tenus exercitus animum bonis artibus non induerat,i. e. only as far as his tongue, only so as to talk,.—Hence, os suum aperire (eccl. Lat.), to begin to speak, ; et saep.: os alicujus aperire,to cause to speak,; cf. ; 3, 27.—But: aperuerunt super me os suum, sicut leo,threatened,: os sublinere alicui, to cheat, befool, v. sublino.—
Esp.: pleno ore, i. e. heartily, zealously: ea nescio quomodo quasi pleniore ore laudamus,.—
Transf.
In gen.: the face, countenance (syn.: vultus, facies), acutis oculis, ore rubicundo,: figura oris,: iratorum,

: in ore sunt omhia, in eo autem ipso dominatus est omnis oculorum,i. e. every thing depends on the countenance,: in tuo ore vultuque acquiesco,: concedas hinc aliquo ab ore eorum aliquantisper,come out from them, out from their presence, leave them alone,. —So of lower animals: insignis et ore Et rutilis clarus squamis,: ore rubicundo (gallina),: ales cristati cantibus oris,: coram in os aliquem laudare,to praise one to his face,: alicui laedere os,to insult one to his face,: praebere os,to expose one's self to personal insults,; so, os praebere ad contumeliam,: in ore parentum liberos jugulat,before their parents' eyes,: quae in ore atque in oculis provinciae gesta sunt,: in ore omnium cotidie versari,: ut esset posteris ante os documentum Persarum sceleris sempiternum,: illos aiunt epulis ante ora positis excruciari fame,: ante ora conjugum omnia pati,.—So of the face, front, as indicative of modesty or impudence: os habet, linguam, perfidiam, = Engl. cheek, : os durum!you brazen face!: os durissimum,very bold,: impudens,: quo redibo ore ad eam, quam contempserim?with what face?; cf. ; ; .—Hence, transf., boldness, effrontery, impudence: quod tandem os est illius patroni, qui, etc.,: nostis os hominis, nostis audaciam,; : non, si Appii os haberem,, a, 2; .—On the contrary: os molle, modest, bashful: nihil erat mollius ore Pompeii,.—

The head: Gorgonis os pulcherrimum, cinctum anguibus,: truncis arborum antefixa ora,. —
Speech (poet.): ora sono discordia signant,.—
A mouth, opening, entrance, aperture, orifice: os lenonis aedium,: porta velut in ore urbis,: ingentem lato dedit ore fenestram,: Ponti,: os atque aditus portus,, § 30: specūs,entrance,: vascula oris angusti,: ulceris,: Tiberis,: venarum,.— Also of the sources of a stream: fontem superare Timavi, Unde per ora novem, etc.,.—
The beak of a ship: ora navium Rostrata,.—
Os leonis, lion's-mouth, a plant, .—
The edge of a sword: interfecit in ore gladii,; et saep.

oscŭlum (auscŭlum, ; osclum, ), i, n.dim.
1. os

la:verb:ostendo.gloss: to expose to view, exhibit, show
senses: to expose to view, exhibit, show
la:verb:ostendo.html:
ostendo, di, sum, and tum (ostensus, Varr. ap. P.; : ostentus, Att. ap. ; Pac. and Varr. ap. Prisc. l. l.; :
ostensurus,; App. ap. P.: ostenturus,; v. also the apoc. form: ostende ostendam, ut permultis aliis exemplis ejus generis manifestum est, Paul. ex Müll.; perh. used by Cato, v. Müll. ad loc., and cf. the letter E), v. a.
obs-tendo
, to stretch out or spread before one; hence, to expose to view, to show, exhibit, display (syn.: monstro, exhibeo).
Lit.
In gen.
Ostendo manus, : os suum populo Romano ostendere audet,: pectora,: umeros,: dentem,: se,to show one's self, appear,: aciem,to display,: equites sese ostendunt,show themselves, appear,. —
Transf.: vocem,to make heard,.—
In partic., to lay open, expose (poet.): Aquiloni glaebas,: lucos Phoebo,: ager qui soli ostentus erit,. —
Trop.
In gen., to show, disclose, exhibit, manifest: ille dies cum gloriā maximā sese nobis ostendat, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 384 Vahl.): non ego illi extemplo ita meum ostendam sensum,: verum hoc facto sese ostendit,he has exposed himself,: sententiam,: potestatem,: spem, metum,i. e. to promise, threaten, et saep.—With two acc.: aliquem nocentem,; cf. Tit. ap. .—Mid., to show itself, appear: nisi cum major spes ostenderetur,.—
In partic.
To show, express, indicate by speech or signs; to give to understand, to declare, say, tell, make known, etc. (syn.: indico, declaro, significo).—With acc.: illud ostendit,.—With obj.- or rel.-clause: ostendit se cum rege colloqui velle,: quid sui consilii sit, ostendit,; cf. .—Absol.: ut ostendimus supra,as we showed above,: sed aliter, atque ostenderam, facio,: signum est per quod ostenditur idonea perficiendi facultas esse quaesita,: primum ostendendum est,.—
To hold up conspicuously, flourish (ironically): sed quaedam mihi magnifica et praeclara ejus defensio ostenditur,.—Hence, osten-tus, a, um, P. a.
Exposed (ante-class.): ager soli ostentus,; so ; ; .—
Subst.: ostentum, i, n.
Lit., a prodigy, wonder, that announces something about to happen, a portent (class.; syn.: monstrum, portentum): praedictiones vero et praesensiones rerum futurarum quid aliud declarant, nisi hominibus ea, quae futura sunt, ostendi, monstrari, portendi, praedici? ex quo illa ostenta, monstra, portenta, prodigia dicuntur,; cf. ; ; .—
Transf., a wondrous thing, prodigy: scis Appium ostenta facere, Cael. ap. : ostenti prorsus genus,.

oscŭlor, ātus, 1 (old form auscŭ-lor, ; ; old
inf. oscularier; v.infra), v. dep.
osculum
, to kiss (class.).
Lit.: compellando blanditer, ausculando. : eam vidisse cum alieno oscularier,kissing each other,: osculari atque amplexari inter se,: ille autem me complexus atque osculans flere prohibebat,: eum complexus, osculatusque dimisit,: simulacrum,: osculetur me osculo oris sui,. —
Transf., to make much of, to value, prize: inimicum meum sic amplexabantur, sic osculabantur,: scientiam juris tamquam filiolam,.

la:noun:Osci.html:
Osci, ōrum, m.,
the Oscans, a primitive people of Campania; in more ancient times called alsoOpiciandOpsci (Obsci), ; cf. Paul. ex Müll. —Hence,
Oscus, a, um, adj., Oscan: ludi,: lingua, Müll.; ; : ludicrum,.—Adv.: Oscē, in Oscan: qui Osce et Volsce fabulantur: nam Latine nesciunt, Titin. ap. Müll.: dicere aliquid, Müll.: scire,.

senses: to show off, make a boastful display of
to hold up as a threat, menace with
la:verb:ostento.html:
ostento, āvi, ātum (
inf. pass. ostentarier, ), 1, v. freq. a.
ostendo
, to present to view, to show, exhibit (class.).
In gen.: alicui jugula sua pro capite alicujus,to present, offer,: aliquem,: campos nitentes,: Sidonias opes,: passum capillum,: liberos,: quo res sapsa loco sese ostentat, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 372 Vahl.).—
In partic.
To show off with vanity or boastfulness, to display, make a display of, boast of, vaunt: amorem tibi meum,: quid me ostentem,why should I make a display of myself?: et prae se ferre,: memoriae ostentandae causā,: clientelas, Dolabell. ap. : triumphos suos,: eum ipsum aliis,: se in aliis rebus,to exhibit themselves,: Ambiorigem ostentant fidei faciundae causā,.—
To hold out or up as an example: desine Tydiden vultuque et murmure nobis Ostentare,.—
To hold out for the purpose of offering or giving; to proffer, promise: alterā manu fert lapidem, panem ostentat alterā,: agrum,: praemia,; ; cf.: praemia modo, modo formidinem,: praedam,.—
To hold out in a threatening manner; to threaten, menace: caedem, servitutem,: periculum capitis,: minas,.—
To show by speech or signs; to indicate, point out, signify, reveal, disclose: (largitio) verbis ostentari potest, re verā fieri, nisi exhausto aerario, nullo pacto potest,: tibi me istis esse familiarem,: principem,to reveal,.—With rel.-clause: ostentans, quanta eos... invidia maneret showing, declaring, .

la:noun:ostium.html:
ostĭum, ii, n.
kindred with Sanscr. oshtha, labium; Slav. ūsta, the same; cf. os
,
a door (class.; cf.: porta, janua, fores, valvae).
Lit.: omnia istaec auscultavi ab ostio,: observare,: rectum ostium, the front-door (cf. posticum), Brix ad loc.: aperire,to open,: operire,to shut,: obserare intus,to bolt,: obdere pessulum ostio,: concrepuit ostium a Glycerio,: inscribat aliquis arse verse in ostio, Afran. ap. Müll.: ostium limenque carceris,: aperto ostio dormire,: quaerere ab ostio,: exactio ostiorum,doortax,; v. 2. ostiarius, III.: sepulcri,.—
Transf., a mouth, an entrance of any kind: Acheruntis ostium in nostrost agro,, 4, 124: aperto ex ostio Alti Acheruntis. Poët. ap. : sacra Inferni ostia,; : ne in rimis areae grana oblitescant, et ostia aperiant muribus ac formicis,entrances,: portūs,: fluminis,mouth,; ; ; ; cf. Rhodani,: Tiberinaque ad ostia venit,; cf. : Oceani,i. e. the Strait of Gibraltar,; .—Fig.: ego sum ostium ovium,.

la:other:Ostia.html:
Ostĭa, ae, f., and Ostĭa, ōrum, n.
ostium; cf. Engl. mouth, in Ply-mouth, Yar-mouth, etc.
,
a seaport town in Latium, at the mouth of the Tiber, built by Ancus Marcius, still called Ostia: Ostiam urbem ad exitum Tiberis in mare fluentis Ancus Marcius rex condidisse fertur, Paul. ex Müll.; cf.: urbs, quam secundum ostium Tiberis (Ancus Marcius) posuit, ex quo etiam Ostiam. id. s. v. Quiritium, p. 254 ib.; Enn. ap. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. quaeso, p. 258 ib. (Ann. v. 145 Vahl.): in ore Tiberis Ostia urbs condita,; .—Form Ostia, ōrum, ; .—Hence,
Ostĭen-sis, e, adj., of or belonging to Ostia, Ostian (class.): Ostiensis ager,; : populus,: quaestor (L. Saturninus),: portus,: provincia,the duty of one of the quœstors to superintend the aqueducts leading to Rome, and the supplying of Rome with corn,; : incommodum,the capture of the Roman fleet by pirates at Ostia,.

ostrum, i, n., = ὄστρεον.

Transf.

la:noun:ostentatio.html:
ostentātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
.
In gen., a showing, exhibition, display (very rare). in armorum magis quam togarum ostentatione, : cognomen Imperiosi ... ab ostentatione saevitiae ascitum,from an open display,.—
In partic.
An idle show, vain display, pomp, parade, ostentation (the predom. signif. of the word): vitanda etiam ingenii ostentationis suspicio,: magnifica et gloriosa,: insolens,: et gloria,: inanis et simulatio,: et venditatio,: sui,.—In plur.: multorum annorum ostentationes meas nunc in discrimen esse adductas, that my many years' boastful promises (of an able administration) are now brought to the test, .—
A false, deceitful show, pretence, simulation, deception: consul veritate, non ostentatione popularis,; cf.: ut in fronte ostentatio sit, intus veritas occultetur,: doloris,feigned pain,: (captivi) producti ostentationis causā,: qui latius ostentationis causā vagarentur,.

oscen, ĭnis, m. (but f. ap. ; ) [obscen, from obs-cano],
a singing-bird, esp. in the auspices; a divining-bird, from whose notes auguries were taken (e. g. the raven, crow, owl): aves aut oscines sunt, aut praepetes: oscines, quae ore futura praedicunt; praepetes, quae volatu augurium significant,; : oscinem corvum prece suscitabo,; ; : Phoebeius,i. e. the crow metamorphosed by Phœbus,.

la:verb:oscito.html:
oscĭto, āre, v. n., and oscĭtor, āri, v. dep. (
inf. oscitarier, Turp. ap. ; or Com. Rel. v. 15 Rib.) [oscieo], to open the mouth wide, to gape.
Of plants, to open, unclose: oscitat in campis caput a cervice revulsum, of the plant lion's-mouth, Enn. ap. ; cf. ; and: (arborum) folia cotidie ad solem oscitant,turn towards the sun,.—
Of living beings, to gape, yawn: ut pandiculans oscitatur,; * : clare ac sonore oscitavit,.— With acc.: quid adhuc oscitamus crapulam hesternam,.—
Trop., to be listless, drowsy, inactive (cf.: dormio. sterto): cum majores (calamitates) impendere videantur, sedetis et oscitamini,i. e. are listless, idle, negligent,; cf. the foll.—Hence, oscĭtans, antis, P. a., listless, sluggish, lazy, negligent (class.): interea oscitantes opprimi,: quae Epicurus oscitans allucinatus est, qs. half asleep, .—Of abstract things: oscitans et dormitans sapientia,.—* Adv.: oscĭtanter, carelessly, negligently: quod ille tam solute egisset, tam leniter, tam oscitanter,.

Of plants, to open, unclose: oscitat in campis caput a cervice revulsum, of the plant lion's-mouth, Enn. ap. ; cf. ; and: (arborum) folia cotidie ad solem oscitant,turn towards the sun,.—
Of living beings, to gape, yawn: ut pandiculans oscitatur,; * : clare ac sonore oscitavit,.— With acc.: quid adhuc oscitamus crapulam hesternam,.—
Trop., to be listless, drowsy, inactive (cf.: dormio. sterto): cum majores (calamitates) impendere videantur, sedetis et oscitamini,i. e. are listless, idle, negligent,; cf. the foll.—Hence, oscĭtans, antis, P. a., listless, sluggish, lazy, negligent (class.): interea oscitantes opprimi,: quae Epicurus oscitans allucinatus est, qs. half asleep, .—Of abstract things: oscitans et dormitans sapientia,.—* Adv.: oscĭtanter, carelessly, negligently: quod ille tam solute egisset, tam leniter, tam oscitanter,.
